“The mighty A100 fleet” will remain mission-capable from 2020 through 2029. Thanks to CUDA, Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell can be continuously upgraded, making them versatile, fungible, highly utilized, rentable, durable, and financeable assets. This directly challenges the narrative that “AI chips become obsolete in 2–3 years.” CoreWeave’s A100 agreement through 2029 supports this as well. The real strength of $NVDA is not the silicon, but the software platform.

$RKLB — New prospectus filed with the SEC: authorization for at-the-market sales of the remaining ~$1.94B under the existing $3B ATM program. This is not a fresh $1.94B. It’s the remaining capacity after approximately $1.056B has already been sold. Purpose: to fund the cash portion of the Iridium acquisition and related expenses (and potentially debt, if needed).

$GOOGL Google co-founder Sergey Brin has been personally pushing the Gemini teams hard in recent months: “Get the model back to the AI frontier.” The goal is clear: close the gap with rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic and put Google back in the lead. Details: • Brin has been back in the office since 2023, writing code, reviewing loss curves, and getting involved in hiring. • February 2025 memo: 60-hour workweeks, being in the office every day, and an aggressive push in the AGI race. • April 2026 Strike Team: an aggressive pivot toward AI agents to close the coding gap with Claude, along with mandatory dogfooding. • August 5–6 reorg: Hassabis stepped back, while Kavukcuoglu and Brin are now leading Gemini from Mountain View. • Last week’s all-hands: employee concerns and changes within the AI unit. Brin doesn’t have an official title, but as he put it, “I poke and prod the team.” He is clearly pushing to bring Google back to the AI frontier. Google remains extremely strong in distribution, while its model leadership appears to be making a comeback. Sources: Reuters, The Information and Financial Times. #Gemini #GoogleAI #SergeyBrin #AGI

$ASTS is trying to solve a problem that no one has truly solved yet: connecting a regular phone directly to a satellite, without the need for a cell tower. Instead of competing for an existing market, they are targeting a massive untapped market. Their agreements with major telecom operators also show that this is being taken seriously. The chart is telling a similar story. After bouncing from the $52–53 bottoming zone, price reclaimed the 20-day moving average and is now testing the upper boundary of the descending channel. A daily close above $77 would completely change the picture.

The main reason I started this page is simple: I don’t want the people who follow me to repeat the mistakes I made when I first entered the markets. When I started trading and investing, I didn’t have anyone to guide me. I had to learn through experience, mistakes, and painful decisions. Looking back, I can honestly say that some of my early success had less to do with how good my decisions were and more to do with the market environment. I was lucky. I entered during an incredible bull market. Prices were rising, liquidity was strong, and the market was forgiving. I made plenty of mistakes, but I didn’t suffer the consequences because the market was moving in my favor. In fact, I ended up making a good return. But there is an important lesson: Being profitable doesn’t always mean you were right. Sometimes the market simply doesn’t punish your mistakes. This is one of the most dangerous things about bull markets. You make a trade, it goes up, and you naturally assume your decision was correct. But sometimes it wasn’t your analysis—the market was simply on your side. When that happens repeatedly, it can create false confidence. You start taking larger positions, using more leverage, ignoring risk management, and believing you can consistently predict the market. Then the market changes. And that is when the real test begins. Markets will not always go up. Not every pullback will become a buying opportunity. Some positions will move against you, and sometimes your biggest losses won’t come from being wrong about direction, but from taking too much risk. That is exactly why I created this page. My goal is not simply to tell people what to buy or sell. I want to share a way of thinking about the markets: risk management, position sizing, patience, discipline, and the ability to recognize when an opportunity is real and when you are simply forcing a trade. Most importantly, I want to emphasize one principle: Protecting your capital comes before making money. Long-term success is not about being right on every trade. Even the best traders have losing positions. The difference is how they manage those losses. A professional trader knows that losses are part of the game when risk is controlled. The real danger is refusing to accept being wrong, adding to losing positions, and allowing a manageable loss to become something that can seriously damage your capital. I wish someone had taught me these lessons when I started. I wish someone had told me that making money in a bull market can be misleading, and that real skill becomes visible when the market turns against you. I don’t want to share only winning trades here. I want to talk about mistakes, bad decisions, poor timing, excessive risk, missed opportunities, and the times when doing nothing was actually the best decision. Because real experience is not built only from profits. I was lucky when I started, and I’m not afraid to admit it. I benefited from a powerful bull market that forgave many of my mistakes. But not everyone will enter the market under such favorable conditions. So I don’t want to sell anyone a story about easy money. The markets are not easy. They only look easy when everything is going up. My goal is to help people develop a process that allows them to protect their capital and make rational decisions through different market conditions. I cannot guarantee anyone financial success. There are no guarantees in the markets. But I can share my experience, my mistakes, and the lessons I’ve learned as honestly as possible. When I started, I didn’t have anyone to guide me. I don’t want the people following me to have to walk the same road alone. My goal is not to tell you what to think. It is to help you learn how to think about the market. Not how to trade more, but how to make better decisions. And if my mistakes can prevent someone else from making the same ones, then every mistake I made was worth something.
